1:
Henry and Wesley make the same two points in nearly the same words, that this is a law of God's making and of his own speaking: God has many ways of speaking to men, by his Spirit, by conscience, by providences, by his voice, but he never spoke at any time upon any occasion as he spoke the ten commandments, which therefore we ought to hear with the more earnest heed. Henry adds that they were uttered not only audibly but with dreadful pomp, and both observe that God had given this law to man before, written in his heart by nature, until sin so defaced the writing that it needed reviving. Ellicott supplies the circumstances from Deuteronomy, that the words were spoken to all the assembly out of the midst of the fire and the cloud and the thick darkness, and that the people did not entreat to be spared further communications until it was over. On the manner of it he declines to go further: how the sounds were produced is a mystery unrevealed, and one on which it is idle to speculate. Jehovah alone appears as the speaker in the Old Testament, while in the New we hear of the instrumentality of angels.

Clarke alone doubts the verse belongs where it stands. He reports Houbigant's conjecture that the words rendered all these words belong to the close of the preceding chapter, so that it was Moses who went down and spake them, and that this chapter properly opens with the bare clause, And God spake, saying. That gives a dignity to the commencement which the longer reading takes away, and the Anglo-Saxon version favours it, having no more than God spoke thus. He then gathers the names the laws have borne: the Ten Words, my Covenant, the moral law, and the Decalogue, which is only the Greek of the first. On the two tables he follows the common reckoning, the first four comprehending the whole system of theology and the last six a system of ethics — a division referring us to the grand principle of love to God and love to man.

What rank the Decalogue holds among moralities is Ellicott's subject. These commandments alone were uttered publicly in the ears of the people, alone inscribed on stone by the finger of God, alone deposited in the innermost place of worship; they formed the very pith and kernel of the covenant, and enunciate a morality infinitely above that of all the then existing nations. There is no compendium of morality in Confucianism, in Buddhism, in the religion of Zoroaster, or of Egypt, or of Greece or Rome, which can be put in competition with it: broad exceedingly, yet searching and minute, embracing the whole range of human duty yet never vague. Gill reaches a similar verdict by another road, calling the ten the best and shortest compendium of morality ever delivered out, except our Lord's own abridgment, and holding that whatever in them is of a moral nature binds all mankind, however plainly the selection suited Israel's case. He passes on the old Jewish notion, which Jarchi delivers as his own, that these words were spoken by God in one word — not grammatically, but as meaning the laws are so compacted as to be inseparable, whence the rule that whoever offends in one point is guilty of all. Calvin will not have the opening counted among the commandments. Many read this verse and the next together as the first, and others take the affirmation for one entire commandment; but since God here neither forbids nor commands anything, and only comes forth in his dignity to claim the authority he deserves, Calvin makes no doubt it is a general preface preparing their minds for obedience — the right of the legislator had first to be established, lest what he commanded should be contemptuously received.
2:
Ellicott states the office of the verse most compactly: the binding nature of commands upon the conscience depends on the authority of the person who issues them, and that there might be no dispute what that authority was, God prefaced the commands themselves with this distinct statement. Gill agrees that the words do not contain the first of the commands but are a preface, showing that God had a right to enact laws for Israel and that they were bound to receive them with reverence — since he is the Lord, the eternal and immutable Jehovah, the Being of beings who gives being to all creatures, and since he was moreover their covenant God in a special and peculiar manner, their King as well as their God, the nation being a theocracy and so more immediately under his government, and having on that account laws preferable to what any other people had. Ellicott adds that the second clause exhibits at once Almighty power and the tenderest compassion and care, since God desires the obedience which springs from love and not from fear.

Wesley sets out the grounds of obligation as three, and binds them into one cord. Because God is the Lord, Jehovah, self-existent, independent, eternal, and the fountain of all being and power, he has an incontestable right to command us. Because he was their God, a God in covenant with them and their God by their own consent, the claim was one they had themselves acknowledged. And because he had brought them out of Egypt, they were bound in gratitude, having been brought out of a grievous slavery into a glorious liberty; by redeeming them he acquired a further right to rule them, so that they owed their service to him to whom they owed their freedom — and thus, Wesley adds, Christ having rescued us out of the bondage of sin is entitled to the best service we can do him. He explains too why the first four commandments stand first: man had a Maker to love before he had a neighbour to love, and justice and charity are acceptable to God only when they flow from the principles of piety. Clarke notices a feature of the grammar that the others pass over — that each individual is addressed here, and not the people collectively, though all are necessarily included, so that each might feel himself bound for himself to hear and do all these words; and he recalls how Moses laboured to impress that personal interest when he said that the Lord made this covenant with us, even us, who are all of us here alive this day.

Two disagreements run under the surface of so short a verse. Keil takes up the question how the words reached the people and answers it flatly: God spake them directly, and not through the medium of his finite spirits, as Hoffmann and Kurtz and others suppose, for there is not a word in the Old Testament about any such mediation. It was Elohim who spoke and who called himself Jehovah, and Deuteronomy says that Jehovah spake to Israel face to face, in the mount, out of the midst of the fire; on the authority of Buxtorf he adds that the Jewish commentators almost unanimously affirm that God himself spoke the words of the decalogue, the sounds being formed in the air by the power of God and not by the intervention or ministry of angels. The second disagreement is over the verse's own standing. Gill takes it for a preface and no part of the first command; Clarke, having called it the preface or introduction, immediately denies the inference, holding that it should not be separated from the commandment which follows.
3:
What the closing words mean is settled by philology. Keil renders them literally beyond me, or in addition to me, giving the Septuagint's apart from me and Luther's by the side of me, and rejects two familiar versions: before me, as the Vulgate has it, is incorrect, and so is against me. Ellicott agrees that before my face means side by side with me, and adds that the singular verb shows the plural form of the divine name to be a mere plural of dignity. Calvin canvasses more alternatives, and rejects the comparative sense, gods whom thou mayest prefer to me, as too frigid: it would make God demand no more than that other gods should not obtain the higher place, whereas he suffers them neither to be likened to him nor joined with him — for religion is corrupted as soon as God's glory is diminished in the least degree. Clarke takes the phrase against the background of the exodus: no strange gods, none that thou art not acquainted with, none who has not given thee such proofs of his power as I have — so that the sense is, in the place of those manifestations which I have made of myself.

The sin in view is not apostasy but admixture. Ellicott states it plainly: God does not suppose that the Israelites, after all he had done for them, would discard him and substitute other gods, but fears the syncretism which would unite his worship with that of other deities. All polytheisms were syncretic and readily enlarged their pantheons, since once the principle of unity is departed from, whether the plurality be greater or less cannot much signify; Israel afterwards fell into the same error, adding the worship of Baal and Ashtoreth without intending to apostatise from Jehovah at all. Calvin makes the same point from the other side: when the Israelites worshipped their Baalim they did not so substitute them for God as to put him aside, yet it was an intolerable profanation to choose patrons in whom some part of the Deity should be lodged. He also fixes the commandment's scope against the one that follows: this precept comprehends the inward worship of God, the next condemning external idolatry, so that men may offend here without statues at all — if any should adore the angels instead of God, none will deny he transgresses; and though such men may evade the eyes of men, their hypocrisy will not escape God. Gill puts the ground simply, that there is but one only living and true God, and all others have only the name and are not by nature gods, being strange even to their own worshippers, who cry to them and get no answer.

How far the commandment reaches is the last question. Clarke holds that it prohibits every species of mental idolatry and all inordinate attachment to earthly things: since God is the fountain of happiness and no creature can be happy but through him, whoever seeks happiness in the creature is necessarily an idolater. The very first commandment, he concludes, is calculated to prevent man's misery and promote his happiness by taking him off from all false dependence. Wesley reaches the same breadth by naming the gods men actually keep: pride makes a god of ourselves, covetousness makes a god of money, sensuality makes a god of the belly — whatever is loved, feared, or depended on more than God, that we make a god of. Henry sets the standard higher still, holding that whatever comes short of perfect love, gratitude, reverence and worship breaks this commandment. Keil closes by observing that the prohibition carries a command inside it: it not only forbids polytheism and the worship of idols in thought, word and deed, but requires the fear, love and worship of God — nearly all the commandments being couched negatively because they presuppose sin.
4:
Whether the commandment forbids images or only their worship divides the commentators sharply. Ellicott reads the two clauses together as one sentence, thou shalt not make any graven image so as to worship it, citing Josephus for the construction; it was not until the days of Hebrew decline, he says, that a narrow literalism pressed the words into an absolute prohibition of painting and sculpture, since Moses himself sanctioned the cherubim above the mercy-seat and the brazen serpent, and Solomon had lions on the steps of his throne. What was forbidden was the worship of God under a material form: the commandment asserts the spirituality of Jehovah. Gill takes the same ground, allowing that images might be made for other uses, as the impressions on coin the Jews did not scruple to handle in Christ's time. Calvin will not have the clauses so joined. He first clears away the opposite error, that all sculptures and pictures are condemned, as a foolish fancy; but he then denies the reading which would allow a visible image of God provided it be not adored — quoting the Douay note which claims images even in the sanctuary are expressly authorised — and holds that to devise any image of God is impious in itself. He grants only that the two parts hang together in practice, since as soon as a man devises an image of God he falls into false worship. Clarke turns the quarrel into a charge: to countenance its image worship the Roman Church has left this commandment out of the decalogue and divided the tenth in two to keep the number, though the verse stands in every manuscript of the Hebrew Pentateuch ever discovered.

On what was worshipped the witnesses are concrete. Clarke works through the Egyptian pantheon the commandment was aimed at: Osiris and Isis supreme; the ox adored as the habitation of Osiris and called Apis, a living beast always kept and the deity supposed to pass at death into another; the ibis and hawk and crocodile besides. Calvin makes the point more briefly, that superstition is never uniform but is drawn aside in various directions, some thinking God represented under the form of fishes and others of birds; so men everywhere lay hold of the materials of error, though God's glory shines on every side.

The sanction — Keil notes that the threat and the promise belong to both commandments, not to the second alone — turns on two words. Of the first Clarke says it shows God's love to this people most expressively, who felt for them as the most affectionate husband could for his spouse, and was jealous for their fidelity because he willed their happiness. Ellicott defines it by contrast: not jealous as some of the Greeks supposed, who thought success or eminence of any kind provoked the deity, but jealous of his own honour, as one who will not see his glory given to another. On the visiting of the fathers' iniquity they part company. Clarke reads it as necessarily implying that the children walk in their fathers' steps, since no man can be condemned by divine justice for a crime of which he was never guilty, and refers it to national judgments — God withdrawing his protection so that the idolatrous Israelites fell into their enemies' hands, which after the Babylonish captivity cured them of idolatry for good. Ellicott takes it as a plain fact of God's natural government: diseases caused by vicious courses are transmitted, a parent's extravagance leaves his children beggars, and to be the son of a felon is to be heavily handicapped in the race of life. Knowing this checks men more than almost anything else; but he bounds the penalty carefully, for it is neither final nor irreversible here, and as respects another world it does not apply at all, since each man will bear his own burden.
6:
Clarke seizes on the arithmetic: what a disproportion between justice and mercy, when justice works to the third or fourth generation and mercy to thousands. Even those who love God merit nothing, so the blessedness they enjoy comes of mercy still. Ellicott renders the word more precisely as to the thousandth generation, which Deuteronomy expresses: God's mercy infinitely transcends his righteous anger, since sin is visited on three or four generations while righteousness advantages descendants for ever. Gill takes the thousands for persons rather than generations, and reads the love required as love shown, by worshipping God only and obeying cheerfully. Clarke makes love the hinge of the law: it would be easier even in Egyptian bondage to make brick without straw than to do the will of God unless his love be shed abroad in the heart.

How far the third commandment reaches is disputed, and Ellicott stands almost alone. The Hebrew is ambiguous, he says, and while some think it forbids profane swearing as well, most modern critics regard it as forbidding false swearing only — a view favoured by our Lord's comment in the Sermon on the Mount, since Christ condemns profane swearing on his own authority, saying, But I say unto you. Calvin argues the other way from the shape of the Decalogue. The word might be rendered for falsehood, and he grants it is so used elsewhere; but since it as often means in vain he prefers that, and observes that perjury is condemned again in the second table, where it injures our neighbours — so the aim of this commandment must be different, that the honour due to God be unsullied. Clarke takes the widest ground: the precept forbids not only false oaths but all common swearing where God's name is used, and even every prayer not accompanied with deep reverence — asking in how many instances it is broken in the prayers of presumptuous worshippers, and reckoning such interjections as O God and good Heavens formal breaches of the law. Gill reports that the Targums restrict the words to swearing by the name of the Lord, to which he thinks the sense may be extended though not limited; Wesley names five ways of offending — hypocrisy, covenant-breaking, rash swearing, false swearing, and using the name lightly.

What is meant by the name is Calvin's own question. It is silly and childish, he says, to restrict the word to the name Jehovah, as if God's majesty were confined to letters or syllables; his essence being invisible, his name is set before us as an image, in so far as he manifests himself and is made known by his own marks, as men are by theirs. On that ground Christ teaches that God's name is comprehended in the heavens, the earth, the temple and the altar, because his glory is conspicuous in them; and the name is profaned whenever any detraction is made from his wisdom, power, justice, truth and clemency — or, more shortly, his name is what Paul calls that which may be known of him. Keil approaches the phrase through the verb, which he insists never means to utter but keeps its sense of taking up or lifting, as one takes up a proverb or lifts a song. On the sanction they are of one mind. Clarke warns that whatever a man may think or hope, God will account him guilty; Wesley observes that magistrates who punish other offences may not think themselves concerned with this one, but that God, jealous for his honour, will not connive at it, and the sinner who holds himself guiltless will find it a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. Ellicott, who confined the commandment to perjury, is correspondingly firm: punishment will overtake the perjured man, if not in this life then in another, for Jehovah will vindicate his own honour.
8:
Only this commandment opens with the word remember, and what it implies divides the commentators. Clarke takes it as pointing back to the creation: this was the most ancient institution, and God calls them to remember it, as if he had said, do not forget that when I finished my creation I instituted the Sabbath. Wesley says the same, that this was not the enacting of a new law but the reviving of an old one. Keil and Ellicott both refuse the inference. Keil grants that remember presupposes an acquaintance with the Sabbath, and that from the history of creation Israel must have known God rested and sanctified the day, but denies it had been kept before: hitherto no commandment had been given to man to sanctify it, and this was given for the first time at Sinai. Ellicott is more cautious, holding that we cannot conclude the Sabbath was a primitive institution, since the reference may be to the injunction lately given about the manna. Gill gives a different reason: the command was of positive institution and no part of the law of nature, and therefore the more liable to be forgotten — all the other laws answering the dictates of nature, which is why no other has remember prefixed.

Whether it still binds is the deeper question, and Calvin and Clarke answer oppositely from a shared premise: both treat the rest as a type. Calvin says God has no delight in idleness, so that there was no importance in the mere cessation of the labours of hands and feet, and it would have been a childish superstition to rest with no other view than to occupy the repose in God's service; the Jews were called away not from every work, since they still circumcised their children that day, but from their own works, that they might wholly devote themselves to God. The sum of the sanctification is the death of the flesh; and this, he insists, was a ceremonial precept, since Paul calls it a shadow whose body is Christ, the substance being exhibited when our old man was crucified with him and we were buried with him. Clarke draws the contrary conclusion from the same typology. Because the commandment is not mentioned in the New Testament as a moral precept, some have presumptuously inferred that there is no Sabbath under the Christian dispensation; but all types are of full force till the thing signified takes place, and the thing signified is that rest in glory which remains for the people of God — therefore its moral obligation must continue till time be swallowed up in eternity. Calvin will not let the precept be thought small, observing that God inculcates no other more frequently, and that when he complains of being despised he says simply that his Sabbaths are polluted.

What keeping the day holy required is Ellicott's subject, and his answer is negative. For the most part the Law insists on abstinence from labour as the main element, and can scarcely be said to prescribe anything positive about the religious employment of the day: the Israelite's attendance at the morning and evening sacrifice was neither required nor expected, and no provision was made for his receiving religious teaching. Probably, he adds, there were always some whom natural piety taught that in the absence of their ordinary employments they should devote themselves to prayer and communion with God — thus only could the day be really kept holy, with a positive and not a merely negative holiness. Wesley notes who was bound: the son and daughter are named and the wife is not, because she is supposed one with her husband, so that if he sanctifies the day she will join him. By keeping it, he adds, the Jews declared that they worshipped the God who made the world, and not gods of their own making.
9:
Whether the six days of labour are commanded, permitted or merely assumed is disputed. Gill takes the clause for a permission and not a precept: it does not enjoin men to work, but grants them six days for their own profit, the Lord reserving one out of seven for his service — a singular favour, that he required no more of their time. Ellicott grants the form is imperative, and reports the view that the commandment prescribes the distribution of a week and enforces the six days' work as much as the seventh day's rest; but he thinks the labour is rather assumed as what will be than required as what must be, so that the clause is prohibitory — thou shalt not work more than six days out of the seven. Clarke takes the strictest line, holding that he who idles away time on any of the six days is as guilty before God as he who works on the Sabbath: no work should be done that can be deferred, works of necessity and mercy alone excepted, and he who works by his servants or cattle is as guilty as if he worked himself.

How far the rest extended is answered by Ellicott and Calvin. Ellicott observes that the whole family was to partake, labour being made to cease rather than devolved by the stronger upon weaker members, and that the rest reached the domestics and the cattle too — for God cares for cattle even for their own sakes. Calvin gives the working rule: what was forbidden was whatever could have been finished yesterday or postponed till to-morrow, so judges might not hear litigants, though a man violently assaulted might be relieved; food might not be cooked for guests, but an ox fallen into a pit was to be taken out. Hence Christ declares that the Sabbath was made for man and not man for the Sabbath. Ellicott traces what came of pressing the negative side too far: by the Maccabees' time it was held unlawful to defend oneself against attack on the Sabbath, and in our Lord's day a rigour was in vogue which his practice was pointedly directed against — and there are parts of Christendom, he adds, where a similar spirit prevails still.

The reason given sends the commentators back to the creation. Ellicott turns the order of explanation around: it is not improbable, he says, that creation was made to occupy six days because one day in seven is the right proportion of rest to labour for man, since God might have created all things in one day had he pleased, but, having the Sabbath in view, prefigured it by spreading his work over six. The law so framed established a conformity between the method of God's working and that of his creatures, and taught men to look on work not as an aimless, weary round but as leading to an end, a rest, a time for rejoicing in the result — each Sabbath a foretaste of that eternal sabbath-keeping which remains for the people of God. Calvin draws a historical inference from the same clause, that the hallowing of the Sabbath was probably prior to the Law: the forbidding to gather manna on the seventh day seems to have arisen from a custom already received, and it is not credible the observance was omitted when God revealed sacrifice to the fathers; what had become extinct among the heathen, God renewed in his Law. Gill dissents on which day it was, denying it can be proved the day appointed to the Jews was the seventh from the creation, and taking it for the seventh from the exodus or from the raining of the manna; he adds that no one day can be kept to exactness of time by all the earth, since it is night with one part while it is day with another.
12:
Which table this commandment belongs to is an old quarrel, which Calvin conducts at length. The usual division he traces to an error of Augustine, who split the precepts of the first table into three on the supposition that their number alluded to the Trinity — a frivolous reason, by trifling with which men have exposed God's law to the mockeries of the ungodly; and those who make only one of the first two must then mangle the last, dividing the prohibition of coveting a neighbour's wife and house into two, though Paul quotes them as one. Because the reverence children pay their parents is accounted a sort of piety, some have placed this precept in the first table; but Christ, Calvin says, ends the controversy by numbering it among the precepts of the second. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion with less heat: it is not of much importance how we divide them, nor is it certain how they were first distributed, but the view that the fifth commandment begins the second table is preferable for its convenience. Gill would extend the parents named to all who stand in their room, and to superiors in office — kings, magistrates, masters and ministers — while holding that it chiefly respects immediate parents; Calvin observes the mother is expressly named lest her sex render her contemptible to her male children.

What honour requires Henry sets out under heads: a decent respect to their persons, of which the contrary is mocking at them; obedience to their lawful commands — come when they call you, go where they send you, do what they bid you — and that cheerfully, so that though you have said we will not, you may afterwards repent and obey; submission to their rebukes, not only to the good and gentle but also to the froward; and endeavouring to make their old age easy. Clarke presses that last head hardest. We can scarcely suppose a man honours his parents who, when they fall weak or blind or sick, does not exert himself to the uttermost in their support; God as truly requires the children to provide for the parents as he required the parents to feed and defend the children in helpless infancy. He adds the rabbinic saying that a man is to honour the Lord with his substance and to honour his father and mother — the Lord so if he have it, his parents whether he have it or not, for if he have nothing he is bound to beg for them.

The promise admits two senses, and Ellicott weighs them. It may guarantee national permanence to a people among whom filial obedience is practised, or mean more simply that obedient children shall as a rule receive long life. For the first he cites Roman and Chinese permanence, and the probability that Israel forfeited Canaan for persisting in the breach of this commandment; for the second, that Paul's application is purely personal and not national, and that the Son of Sirach expounds it the same way. He adds that an Egyptian sage writing long before Moses declared from experience that the son who attends to his father's words will grow old in consequence. Clarke draws the darker inference from the Deuteronomy form of the promise: if it is that it may go well with thee, it will go ill with the disobedient, and the untimely deaths of many young persons are the judicial consequence of disobedience to parents — most who come to an untimely end being obliged to confess that this, with the breach of the Sabbath, was the principal cause of their ruin. Henry and Wesley soften the terms without weakening them: those who keep this commandment shall live as long on earth as infinite wisdom sees good, and whatever they seem cut short of here shall be made up in eternal life, the heavenly Canaan.
13:
Ellicott explains why the sixth commandment is stated so bluntly. The security of life is the primary object of government, men having coalesced into states for self-preservation; all written codes forbid murder, and where there are none an unwritten law does. What distinguishes the Mosaic legislation, he says, is the care it afterwards takes to separate murder from manslaughter, from death by misadventure, and from justifiable homicide — but before those distinctions could be drawn the sanctity of human life had to be broadly laid down, so the law was given in the widest terms and the exceptions reserved till later. Keil sets the commandment in the order of the table, following Luther: the five words that follow secure life, marriage and property against active attack, and then, passing from deed to word and thought, forbid false witness and coveting. Luther's note, which he quotes, runs from the greatest injury to the least: the killing of a man, the violation of his wife, the taking of his goods, and, for those who cannot hurt so, the tongue, or failing that the heart. That the table advances to desire proves, Keil adds, that the deed is not to be separated from the disposition, and that the law is fulfilled only when the heart itself is sanctified.

Calvin lays down the rule governing all such precepts: in negative commandments the opposite affirmation is also to be understood, since otherwise a man would satisfy God's law by merely abstaining. There are two parts to it: that we should not vex or oppress any, and that we should aid the miserable who are unjustly oppressed, and resist the wicked lest they injure men as they list. With God anger is accounted murder, and concealed hatred too, since whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer; and when Christ says as much he is not framing a new law, as some have ignorantly supposed, but showing the folly of interpreters who insist only on the husk of things. Clarke works the same breadth into particulars, reckoning under this commandment not only all actions by which life may be abridged, but all wars for extending empire or commerce, all sanguinary laws by which men die for trifling offences, and all dispositions that lead men to meditate mischief. Gill keeps the ordinary exceptions — lawful war, self-defence, the magistrate's execution of malefactors — but adds to the crimes forbidden the stabbing of a man's character.

On the seventh commandment Ellicott gives the social reason first: next to respecting a man's life comes respecting his domestic peace, adultery being an invasion of the household and a dissolution of the contract which is the main basis of social order. What is peculiar in the Mosaic enactments is the absolute equality on which they place the man and the woman: adulterers are as hateful as adulteresses and as surely to be put to death, for with God there is no respect of persons and no respect of sexes. Whether it reaches beyond adultery proper is Calvin's question, and he answers with heat. If the Law is a perfect rule of holy living it would be absurd to suppose it gave a licence for fornication with adultery alone excepted; those who have sought a reputation for acuteness by granting that fornication is condemned in the New Testament but not in the Law have done nothing but betray their disgraceful ignorance. Since God is declared to have blessed marriage, it follows that the connection of male and female outside marriage is accursed. Gill reports the same question from the Jewish side, that strictly the word means only the sin with another man's wife, as Jarchi observes, though Aben Ezra takes it for the wider term; he extends the prohibition to unchaste thoughts no less than acts, as Wesley does in a sentence, that it forbids all uncleanness with the desires which produce it.
15:
Ellicott grounds the eighth commandment in something older than law. The framers of Utopias have imagined communities without private property, but such a thing has never been realised, and the laws of all known States recognise it; here law has but embodied natural instinct — the savage who hammers out a flint knife by repeated blows with a pebble, labouring long and undergoing pain, feels the implement he has made is his own and his right to it indisputable. Calvin defines the crime from charity, the end of the Law: every man's rights should be preserved, so that not only those are thieves who secretly steal but those who seek gain from the loss of others. God uses the word theft, he says, because all naturally abhor it as disgraceful, and men bury their misdeeds under so many coverings, craft and low cunning being called prudence. Since the world boasts of vices as though they were virtues, God wipes away the gloss when he pronounces every unjust means of gain to be so many thefts. Clarke widens the charge, holding that all kidnapping and slave-dealing fall under this law whether practised by individuals or by the state, since a state that enacts bad laws is as criminal before God as the individual who breaks good ones. Gill catalogues the kinds — highway robbery, domestic theft, sacrilege, and the stealing of men to make slaves of them — while Wesley adds that a man may rob himself by sinful spending or sparing.

Clarke and Ellicott reach for the same lines of Shakespeare, and put them to different uses. Clarke quotes them at the eighth commandment, on the supposition that depriving a man of his good name is a kind of theft: who steals my purse steals trash, but he that filches from me my good name robs me of that which not enriches him, and makes me poor indeed. Ellicott quotes them at the ninth, as indicating that calumny may injure a man more than robbery. What he finds peculiar to the Hebrew legislation is its reach: false witness is worst in a court of justice, and that offence has generally been punishable by law, but this code denounced also the commoner practice of spreading untrue reports, and afterwards added a distinct prohibition of raising a false report. Calvin argues the same breadth from the order of the commandments: it would be absurd that God, having shown that men's fortunes are cared for by him, should neglect their reputation, which is much more precious — so that however we defame our neighbours, in the streets or in secret corners, we are accounted false witnesses before him.

Calvin presses the commandment further than truth alone will carry it. It is not enough to restrain the tongue unless we are also candid interpreters of our neighbours' acts and words; and God forbids not only inventing accusations against the innocent but giving currency to reproaches out of malevolence. A man may deserve his ill name, and the charge may be true; but if the reproach is the ebullition of our anger, it is vain to plead that we have advanced nothing but what is true — for Solomon says that love covereth many sins whereas hatred brings reproaches to light. Nor may we be too curious in observing the defects of others; and we must close our ears as well as our mouths, for he who listens eagerly to sinister reports about his brother is as injurious as the man who maligns him. Clarke pushes the rule to its limit: he who bears false testimony against even the devil himself comes under the curse of this law, because his testimony is false; and by neighbour, he adds, any human being is intended, enemy or friend. Wesley names the motive running through them all: the endeavour to raise our own reputation upon our neighbour's ruin.
17:
Calvin raises the objection before answering it. If the inward purity of the heart is everywhere required — so that under adultery secret unchastity is forbidden and under theft every unlawful appetite for gain — why forbid the lust for theft and fornication separately? It looks a superfluous repetition, absurd in ten short precepts wherein God has embraced the whole rule of life. His answer is that men's hypocrisy is such that they had to be pressed more closely, lest they seek subterfuges under pretence that the doctrine was obscure: had they heard only thou shalt not kill, nor commit fornication, nor steal, they might have thought their duty fully performed by outward observance. So, after laying down rules for moral integrity broadly, God at length ascends to the fountain itself, and points out the root from which all the evil and corrupt fruits spring. Ellicott makes the point historically. The commandment was added, he says, to teach that the Law concerns not acts and words only but the thoughts of the heart — rightly understood, the seventh and eighth commandments already contain the tenth. But ancient moralists did not usually recognise this: thought, unless carried into acts, was regarded as free, and no responsibility was held to attach to it. It was therefore of importance that the divine Law should assert a control over men's thoughts, since these are the source of all evil in word and deed.

Gill draws the conclusion that gives the commandment its force: the motions it forbids would not be known, or thought sinful, but for this law — nor are they known even by it until the Spirit of God uses it to convince men of them. Not only the schemes of sin in the mind are forbidden, but its first risings in the heart, motions not assented to which spring up unawares from the corruption of nature; which shows the spirituality of the law and the impossibility of its being perfectly kept by fallen men. Calvin illustrates the effect from the one man who recorded it. Paul gathers from this commandment that the whole Law is spiritual, since God by condemning lust showed he had not merely imposed obedience on our hands and feet but restrained our minds; and Paul confesses he was awakened by this single word. Being blameless in the eyes of men, he had been persuaded he was righteous before God, and was alive, as Calvin puts it, as if the Law were absent or dead; but when he perceived what the commandment against coveting meant, the dead Law was raised to life and he died — convinced he was a transgressor, and seeing the curse overhanging him.

How early the offence begins is Calvin's last question, and he sets the mark early. Something more is expressed by coveting than a bare act of will: the flesh tempts us to wish for this or that, so that the evil concupiscence betrays itself although consent has not been added; and since the sin of the will was already condemned, God here restrains evil desires before they prevail. James marks the same steps: lust conceives before it begets sin, and sin when finished brings forth death. Clarke describes the same thing from the outside, taking covet to mean longing after a person or thing in order to enjoy it as a property: the command is broken by the man who lusts after his neighbour's wife and works to ingratiate himself into her affections and to lessen her husband in her esteem. Wesley marks the difference between this commandment and those before: they forbid all desire of doing what would injure our neighbour, this all inordinate desire of having what would gratify ourselves — O that such a man's house were mine, such a man's estate mine — the language of discontent at our own lot and envy at our neighbour's.
18:
Henry asks why the law was given so dreadfully and answers three ways: it was designed to give a sensible discovery of the majesty of God, that knowing the terror of the Lord we might live in his fear; it was a specimen of the terrors of the general judgment, in which sinners will be called to account for the breach of this very law; and it was an indication of those convictions which the law brings into the conscience, to prepare the soul for the gospel. The law was given, he concludes, in such a way as might startle and humble men, so that the grace and truth which came by Jesus Christ might be the more welcome — which is why the apostle sets the scene out as a foil to the liberty of the New Testament. Clarke suggests how the terror was administered: the people had witnessed these things before, but here they seem repeated, probably with a peal of thunder and a gleam of lightning at the end of each command, to impress their hearts with the holiness of the law. Gill notices that the people are said to have seen the thunderings, and explains it as one sense put for another, Augustine having observed that to see is used in Scripture of all five senses.

What the people did next Henry and Wesley read as a cure. Before God began to speak they had been thrusting forward to gaze, but now they were cured of their presumption and taught to keep their distance; and in begging that God would speak by Moses they obliged themselves to acquiesce in his mediation, nominating him themselves and promising to hearken to him as God's messenger. Henry draws the lesson hard. Once God tried speaking to men immediately, and it was found they could not bear it: it rather drove men from God than brought them to him, and though it terrified them it did not deter them from idolatry, since soon after this they worshipped the golden calf. Let us therefore rest satisfied with the instruction given us by the scriptures and the ministry, for if we believe not them, neither should we be persuaded though God spoke to us in thunder as he did from Sinai. Clarke turns the episode forward instead of back: it teaches the absolute necessity of that great Mediator between God and man, Christ Jesus, since no man comes to the Father but by him.

Moses answers with what looks a contradiction, which Clarke states as a maxim: fear not, that ye may fear. The fear forbidden brings consternation into the soul and produces nothing but terror; the fear enjoined is what reverence and filial affection inspire — and he sets the two against each other, since he who fears in the first sense can neither love nor obey, while he who fears not in the second falls under the first temptation that occurs. Henry and Wesley describe the forbidden fear in the same terms, as the fear which has torment and genders to bondage, over against a standing reverence of God's majesty. Keil traces the pastoral order of the words: Moses first took away the false fear of death by the answer, fear not, then gave the reason, for God is come to prove you — the proving being a testing of the heart, so that by this display of his glory God might inspire the true fear of himself. Ellicott catches what is remarkable in the closing tableau: the same manifestation which repelled the people attracted Moses. Wesley presses the verb — he was made to draw near, so the word is — and adds that Moses of himself durst never have ventured into the thick darkness if God had not called him, some rabbins supposing that an angel was sent to take him by the hand and lead him up.
22:
Clarke takes the words about speaking from heaven as evidence, not description. Though God manifested himself by the fire and the thick darkness, the ten words were probably uttered from the higher regions of the air, and that, he argues, proves there was no imposture: strange appearances might be counterfeited on earth, as the magicians of Egypt had often done, but it would be impossible to represent a voice carrying a long series of instruction as proceeding from heaven itself — which is why Moses could afterwards appeal to the people upon a fact incontrovertible. Keil draws a different inference from the same clause: Jehovah came down on Sinai enveloped in the darkness of a cloud, and thereby made known that his nature was heavenly and could not be imitated in any earthly material. Ellicott notices what the sentence does structurally: it identifies the giver of the Book of the Covenant with the deliverer of the Ten Commandments.

Why the second commandment is repeated here Henry answers two ways. It may point to what God chiefly had in view, their peculiar addictedness to idolatry: ten commandments God had given them, but Moses is ordered to inculcate especially the first two — they must not forget any, but must be sure to remember those. Or it may point to what could be inferred from the manner of God's speaking, since he had given sufficient demonstration of his presence and they needed no images of him as though absent; besides which they had seen no manner of similitude, and his manifesting himself by a voice alone showed that they were to keep up communion with him by his word and not otherwise. Gill arrives at the same reading by the grammar. The Talmudists and Jarchi supply the elliptical clause as meaning that they should make no likeness of God's ministers on high, the angels or the stars; but Gill prefers to render it, ye shall not make any likeness of me, since they had seen only the cloud and the fire. Wesley gives the reason in a line: they were more addicted to idolatry than to any other sin.

On the phrase make with me they part company. Henry builds two arguments on it: that by such images they would affront God, since though they pretended to worship them only as representations of him they really made them rivals with him; and that they would abuse themselves, since while they thought to assist their devotion they would corrupt it and put a cheat upon themselves. Clarke marks the change of preposition, that where the first commandment said no other gods before me, this says none with me, as emblems kept up to preserve the memory of his magnificence; whereas God would have only an altar of plain turf, on which they should offer the sacrifices that commemorate their own guilt and the need of an atonement. Ellicott alone finds nothing in the words, holding the expression unusual but of no peculiar force; what he finds significant is the choice of metals. Gods of silver and gold are specially forbidden because it was to idolatry of just this kind that the Israelites were inclined, the golden calf being no isolated phenomenon: molten images were objects of worship throughout the ages before the Captivity. The animal worship of Egypt had no attractions for the Hebrews; they did not offer to images of stone or marble like the Greeks, still less bow down to stocks like the heathen around them — the molten image was the form of idol which had most charms for them, and the more precious the material the better satisfied they were to worship it. Keil supplies the reason such images are condemned even when meant well: intended as symbols of Jehovah, they became false gods from the very fact that they were meant as representations of a purely spiritual God.
24:
Why the altar was to be of earth or rough stone Calvin explains by what would be left behind. God would have them built of earth so that they might fall down of themselves and no trace remain after the people departed; and if stones were used he forbade their being fitted into a permanent structure, lest the appearance entice posterity to superstition. We know, Calvin says, how antiquity and the example of our forefathers attract the minds of the vulgar: had anything in the shape of an altar remained, religious notions would at once have attached to it, that God could nowhere be better worshipped than in a place dedicated of old by their fathers. He is impatient of readings that look for more, surprised that commentators should invent allegories here. Gill supplies the practical description — turfs of earth, quickly thrown up as their travels required and as easily thrown down after — and adds from Tertullian that the Romans under Numa had neither images nor temples, but only altars of turf. He also passes on Ainsworth's figure, that the altar of earth represented Christ's human nature — the very reading Calvin complains of. Ellicott gives the historical shape of the command: the earliest altars were of earth or unhewn stones, built with little labour and no tools, but as civilisation advanced it became usual to erect altars of hewn stone adorned with carvings, in which human and animal forms were often introduced.

Wesley puts it sharply: that they might not be tempted to think of a graven image, they were not so much as to hew the stones into shape, but to pile them as they were. Clarke adds a reason of circumstance and one of principle: they were wanderers with no fixed residence, so no time should be wasted on costly altars soon to be left behind; and the altar itself, costly or mean, was nothing in the worship — only the place on which the victim should be laid. Keil supplies the positive idea behind the rule: the altar, as an elevation built of earth or rough stones, was a symbol of the elevation of man to God, who is enthroned on high — man raising himself to God in his sacrifices, yet by an altar only of earth, or if of stones then not of hewn ones, since if he swings his tool over it he defiles it. Ellicott observes that stone altars are not absolutely prohibited, since the Israelites use them afterwards; God forbids only the shaping of the stones. On the pollution the tool would cause Ellicott offers a reason of his own: nature is God's handiwork and therefore pure, man by contact imparts his own impurity, and the altar whereby sin was expiated had to be free from human taint.

The promise attached to the altar draws the warmest comment. Clarke takes the words to mean wherever God is worshipped, whether in the wilderness, at the tabernacle or in the temple, and finds them equivalent to our Lord's saying that where two or three are gathered in his name he is in the midst of them — adding that since it was Jesus who was the angel that spoke in the wilderness, the promise in the law and that in the gospel proceeded from the same mouth. Wesley reads it as where my name is recorded, that is, where I am worshipped in sincerity. Calvin thinks the second half of the verse has been ignorantly perverted by commentators, who read it with the first as though God had forbidden such an altar on Mount Zion too; whereas he is answering a doubt — will God be favourable to us where he heard our fathers' prayers? The answer is that they will pray duly if only they obey his command and seek no other place than the one he shall choose.
26:
The reason given for the prohibition is decency, which Calvin sets in the context of the priests' conduct. God had already prescribed modesty to them in their private actions and required that they wear drawers when they went into the sanctuary; but not content with that symbol of purity, he forbids them to ascend by steps, lest the drawers themselves should be seen and the dignity of sacred things be impaired. By every means, Calvin concludes, God would induce the Israelites to conduct themselves purely and chastely in the exercises of religion. Gill notes that the command is addressed to the priests, as the Targums paraphrase it, and explains the danger plainly: the part which is not to be named would be exposed if there were many steps set at a distance from each other. The altar built with the tabernacle, he observes, was only three cubits high and needed no steps; the difficulty arises only with the later altar.

What was done once altars grew taller is answered three ways. Gill reports the Jewish solution, that Solomon's altar being ten cubits high some ascent was necessary, and there was what they called a Kibbesh — a causeway of earth rising gradually to the top, some thirty-two cubits long and sixteen broad; and the Targum of Jonathan paraphrases the words as meaning they go up not by steps but by bridges. Wesley reaches the same conclusion independently, granting that God afterwards appointed an altar ten cubits high but thinking they went up not by steps but by a sloping ascent. Ellicott takes the other course. Once the priests' dress had been so arranged that no exposure was possible, this precept became unnecessary — from which it would seem that Solomon's altar simply had steps, as comparing Chronicles with Ezekiel suggests.

Clarke stands back to ask why the altars were low and plain at all. The English word comes from a root meaning high, though the Hebrew, from a verb meaning to slay, signifies merely a place for sacrifice; it was the heathen, imitating the rites of the true God in their idolatrous worship, who made their altars very high and so gave them the name of elevated places — building them so partly through pride, and partly that their gods might the better hear them. Hence come the high places so severely condemned in Scripture; some have even imagined that the pyramids were altars of this kind. God therefore ordered his own to be either of simple turf, so that there might be no expense the people could ill afford and no incentive to idolatry from a costly structure; or of unhewn stone, so that no images of animals or of the heavenly bodies might be sculptured on them, as among the Egyptians, whose ancient altars still testify it — and those carved images became in time incentives to idolatry and even objects of worship. In short, Clarke concludes, God formed every part of his worship so that everything belonging to it might be as dissimilar as possible from that of the surrounding nations, and especially the Egyptians, from whose land they had just departed; and this seems the whole design of statutes on which commentators have written learnedly, imagining difficulties where probably there are none. He ends by looking back over the chapter. Here, he says, we have met with some of the most awful displays of the divine Majesty, manifestations which have no parallel and can have none until he appears in glory to judge the quick and the dead. The glory was terrible, and to the children of Israel insufferable; and yet how highly privileged they were to have God himself speaking from the midst of the fire, and giving them statutes so righteous and so pure that they have been the admiration of the wise and upright in every age where their voice has been heard.
